title: Dawud and Sulayman judge a field
hookLine: a flock ruins a field, and Sulayman is given the better understanding (21:78–79)

lines: THE FARMER GOES TO THE KING.
cards: A farmer walks out to his field one morning, and it's gone. Not stolen. Eaten.

Overnight, someone's flock wandered in and grazed it down to the dirt: a season's work, a family's food. The farmer goes to the king for justice. The king is Dawud, a prophet well-known for his wisdom.
Sitting beside him is his son, Sulayman, still young. Al-Anbiya tells the case in two verses.

teach.b: The Qur'an gives the bare outline: Dawud and Sulayman judging about the field, when the people's sheep grazed it by night, and We were witness to their judgment.
Then, in Pickthall's words: "And We made Solomon to understand (the case); and unto each of them We gave judgment and knowledge."
Commentators, drawing on reports from companions like Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, fill in the details.

teach.h: DAWUD: THE FLOCK FOR THE FIELD.
teach.b: Dawud ruled first: the sheep go to the owner of the field, as payment for the loss. Fair enough. Then Sulayman, some reports say he was about eleven, suggested another way.

teach.h: SULAYMAN: MILK FOR NOW, FIELD REGROWN.
teach.b: Let the farmer keep the sheep for a while and live off their milk and wool, while the shepherd works the field until it grows back to what it was. Then each takes back his own.
Nobody loses everything, and the harm is actually repaired. Dawud agreed, and changed his ruling.
Now the second half of the verse: to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge. The Qur'an doesn't shame the father. Both were wise; on this case, the younger saw further.
A hadith in Bukhari tells of a judge who works hard to reach the right ruling: if he's right, he gets two rewards, and if he's wrong, still one.
Another hadith in Bukhari has the two of them again: two women claim one baby, Dawud gives it to the elder, and Sulayman calls for a knife to divide it.
The younger woman cries out, give it to her, and he knows she's the mother. In both stories the younger one sees further, and in the field case, a father listens and lets his son be right.

how: Muslim scholars cite 21:78–79 when teaching that judges may differ and revise rulings, and that both the careful judge who errs and the one who is right are rewarded; teachers also use it to show respect for the young.

games.q: you're the young Sulayman. your father has ruled that the sheep go to the farmer. you see a way that repairs the field. what do you propose?
o: the farmer keeps the sheep forever.
the farmer uses the sheep's milk and wool while the shepherd regrows the field, then each takes back his own.
the shepherd pays a fine to the king.
games.why: milk and wool for the farmer for now, work for the shepherd until the field regrows, then each takes back his own. Dawud agreed.

practice: Think of a problem you're working on, at home, at work, in your community, and of someone younger who knows something about it: a child, a niece, a new coworker, a student.
Picture asking them what they'd do, and really listening, the way Dawud listened. What might they see that you've stopped noticing?

wordCard.voice: Sulayman. The young son whose ruling about the grazed field showed deeper wisdom than his father's, and which his father accepted. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: and We made Sulayman understand it (21:79).

carryVoice: Your line: the young one saw it. Wisdom doesn't always wait for age. Day four hundred eighty-one, done.
